records.title: Four Maricopa County property waitlists will close December 1
records.label: Housing Authority of Maricopa County · Dated property-waitlist notice
summary: The Housing Authority of Maricopa County says it will stop accepting applications for four property waitlists at 8 a.m. Arizona time on December 1, 2026, until further notice.
The notice names Casa Bonitas Apartments, Clare Feldstadt Apartments in Mesa, Heritage at Surprise Apartments, and Heritage Senior Apartments in Surprise. Paper applications will not be accepted.
The notice was located during the latest review; it was not newly issued.
caveats: Keep in mind. Property-specific application limits may apply earlier. Check HAMC’s latest schedule before applying. This notice does not guarantee an apartment or change the City of Phoenix’s housing programs.
notes: Scope Four HAMC property waitlists, separate from City of Phoenix programs Source dates October 2026 closure notice and November 5, 2026 waitlist schedule; checked November 9, 2026 Arizona time

records.label: Phoenix city · Draft FY2025–26 report · Unresolved wording

summary: The County estimates $768,000 for HOME Urban County and $667,529 for Community Housing Development Organizations. Both competitions exclude the City of Phoenix. Applications are due December 8, 2026 at 5 p.m.

records.title: Girasol: redevelopment and dated progress
records.label: Planned gross redevelopment units; not completed production · Construction progress and forecasts as of October 26, 2026
summary: Girasol, the final Edison-Eastlake phase on the former 145-unit Sidney P. Osborn site, is planned for 364 apartments: 289 affordable and 75 market-rate.

The October 26, 2026 update reported Girasol Phase I construction 82% complete and Phase II 79% complete. It forecast their move-ins in early 2027, Phase III construction in Q1 2027 and Phase III move-ins in 2028.

records.title: Capital Fund: obligation, draw and expenditure definitions
records.label: HUD program definitions · Not Phoenix transaction evidence
summary: PHA obligation: a binding agreement for work or financing that will result in outlays.
Grant draw: Capital Funds vouchered through HUD’s Line of Credit Control System (LOCCS).
HUD grant-reporting expenditure: the PHA pays a contractor or vendor bill using funds disbursed from LOCCS.
caveats: What this does not show A PHA obligation is different from HUD’s federal award obligation. This HUD grant-reporting definition of expenditure is distinct from the SEFA accounting measure. These definitions do not establish Phoenix’s amounts, dates or completion of grant-processing requirements.
notes: Scope HUD Capital Fund guidance for public housing agencies (PHAs); national definitions, not a Phoenix ledger. Period and source date HUD training materials dated September 25, 2023.
Financial stage: Definitions separating a PHA commitment, a grant disbursement and expenditure.

What Still Needs Explaining in CDBG Spending? Documented: The corrected PR-26’s resources, spending and ending balance add up. records.title: What Do Housing First’s Results Tell Us?
records.label: Q-017 · FY2026; measure-specific cohorts
summary: Documented: Housing First recorded 21 permanent-housing exits among 36 counted leavers (58.3%), after excluding eight of 44 leavers, and all 26 openings filled through Coordinated Entry for July 1, 2025–June 1, 2026. Separately, seven of 43 people in the June 1, 2024–June 1, 2025 permanent-housing exit cohort returned within 12 months (16.3%). These are different groups and periods; weighted scores are not housing-success percentages or evidence of underspending.
caveats: Unknown: The aggregate destination categories accounting for the eight excluded exits are not established. Later aggregate outcomes and costs for comparable groups and reporting periods also remain unverified.

summary: Pima County approved $8.7 million for housing and stability programs. A separate $1 million request was tabled indefinitely. The County also approved $2.99 million in PRICE agreement scopes for home repairs and eviction assistance. These approvals and targets do not establish actual County spending or households served.
caveats: Pima County approved $8.7 million for housing and stability programs. A separate $1 million request was tabled indefinitely. The County also approved $2.99 million in PRICE agreement scopes for home repairs and eviction assistance. These approvals and targets do not establish actual County spending or households served.

On September 8, 2026, the Board approved $5 million for gap funding and $3.7 million for housing stability, totaling $8.7 million for FY2027. The separate additional $1 million request was tabled indefinitely. These are allocation decisions, not evidence of payments or completed assistance. The posted meeting summary expressly is not approved minutes. Meeting summary, PDF p. 6 · Official allocation action

The two County-approved PRICE agreements total $2,986,331: $2,009,932 for home repairs and $976,399 for eviction-prevention and legal services. Their stated term is July 1, 2026–June 30, 2029. These are components of existing PRICE grant funding, not additional federal revenue to add to the full award. Repair agreement · Eviction-prevention agreement · Repair approval · Eviction-prevention approval

The records identify planned work and targets. They do not establish completed repairs, actual payments, legal outcomes or households already assisted. The posted execution pages contain blank mayor, Board chair and clerk signature lines; attorney review is present. Fully executed counterparts and later amendments remain unverified. Blank lines in a posted packet do not prove that no agreement was later executed.

Separately, USAspending reports $78,172.27 in cumulative federal outlays for the City of Tucson’s $11,519,567.21 PRICE award, B-23-PR-04-0001. The latest returned reporting period is August 2026, before the September County approvals. This is not a measure of County spending. Monthly cumulative outlay rows must not be added together. The database’s later update stamp is not the expenditure cutoff. Federal award and reporting-period record

Later expenditures and actual household outcomes remain unverified. The difference between the award and reported outlays is not a verified available balance, and these records alone do not establish improper withholding or misuse.

summary: Additional public records provide more precise checkpoints for Tucson and Pima County housing programs. They strengthen the evidence while keeping accounting, occupancy and outcome questions open.
caveats: The October 20 PHA report records $49,539,339 in Tucson and $9,161,950 in Pima County payments to property owners or managers for FY2026 (July 1, 2025–June 30, 2026), totaling $58,701,289. It reports $614,215 plus $306,275, totaling $920,490, as unaudited unspent assistance or next-year reserves, while its narrative calls the amount an operating surplus. Those labels still need reconciliation. October 20 report, pp. 1–2

The FY2025 Single Audit separately reports $62,789,037 in Housing Choice Voucher federal expenditures for July 1, 2024–June 30, 2025. Its accrual or modified-accrual measure is not FY2026 cash receipts. The near-match to the draft’s approximately $62.8 million narrative is a source-year question, not proof of an error. FY2025 Single Audit

Q-010 remains open: match FY2026 receipts, assistance payments, administration and restricted-reserve roll-forwards, and clarify the carryover labels. These comparisons do not establish available assistance or missing money.

The October 16 announcement’s 24 apartments and 25 households remain unreconciled. Neither the permit register nor the later narrative verifies a completed move count, new admissions or current vacancies. The original certificate and any conditions or renewal still need verification.

The separate 14th-floor application TC-CFO-1126-00224 remains Submitted – Online in the register checked November 7. November 6 inspection notes permit an application; they do not establish an issued certificate. Permit displays may lag: the 15th-floor register’s embedded data stamp is November 5. 14th-floor application

The action report does not supply the closing package or precise closing date, signed assistance contracts or actual Flats occupancy. The published County packet has blank signature and covenant lines; executed documents, completion reporting and certificates of occupancy remain record targets. The motel award must not be added to the Flats construction budget.

The TPCH FY2026 scorecard reports 17 of 24 County One Stop rapid-rehousing leavers exiting to permanent housing (70.8%) for July 1, 2025–June 1, 2026, with no excluded leavers. A separate earlier group had 13 of 24 people return to homelessness within 12 months (54.2%); that cohort exited to permanent housing during June 1, 2024–June 1, 2025. TPCH scorecard, Data Back Up row 18

These are people in one project and two different cohorts, not a Countywide success rate or one group’s retention result. Matched reporting periods, inclusion rules and aggregate follow-up outcomes are needed before comparing costs or broader program performance.

HUD’s HOME match workbook, FY2024 sheet row 24, lists a 50% fiscal-distress reduction for the Tucson Consortium, supporting a 12.5% required match rate. This does not validate accumulated match-credit eligibility or make credits available cash. HUD HOME match workbook

The original PY2024 Annual Action Plan describes the rapid-rehousing target as 30 individuals in its project narrative but 30 households in its goal table; another entry gives 10 households for combined rapid rehousing and prevention. The comparison with 18 reported actual households therefore needs a clarified target definition. Original action plan

The CAPER’s PR-91 shows the entire $48,734 rapid-rehousing budget drawn by September 23, 2025. That later grant-draw checkpoint does not explain the outcome count or establish cost per household. CAPER and PR-91

Definition clarification: Earlier current summaries called the ESG target simply “30 households.” The original plan uses both people and households. Q-004 now keeps that uncertainty explicit; the historical records remain available.

A reconciled table and an explanation of the counts and calculations would clarify the results. The discrepancies alone do not establish misuse of funds.

summary: We withdrew the earlier $944,972.60 comparison because it combined regular CDBG and CDBG-CV, which are reported separately. The $1,284,589.71 difference within regular CDBG remains unexplained; it does not establish missing funds.
caveats: We withdrew the earlier $944,972.60 comparison because it combined regular CDBG and CDBG-CV, which are reported separately. The $1,284,589.71 difference within regular CDBG remains unexplained; it does not establish missing funds.
Summary revised: November 6, 2026, 9:52 a.m. MST (Tucson). Original correction history and source dates follow unchanged.

The resource figures and ending balance in Tucson’s CDBG reports add up. The remaining question is more focused: how does the City’s spending narrative connect to the corrected financial report for its regular CDBG program? Federal guidance now helps separate that question from coronavirus-response funding. Financial summary · Spending narrative · OMB reporting guidance, PDF p. 61
Those calculations reproduce the City’s resource total and ending balance. The reported balance does not establish money available for new work today. Corrected PR-26, PDF p. 149

The summary table’s $4,717,936 agrees with the corrected PR-26 after rounding. The narrative says the final CDBG draw occurred after June 30, 2025, which may help explain the difference. But the records reviewed do not show which transactions connect the two figures or establish that timing explains the full amount. Summary table and narrative, PDF p. 13 · Corrected PR-26, PDF p. 149

That calculation subtracted both the $3,433,346.66 CDBG narrative and the $339,616.74 CDBG-CV narrative from the rounded $4,717,936 summary total. It mixed the separately reported grant programs. In light of the federal reporting guidance, it should not be presented as a second comparable spending gap. The question to pursue is the $1,284,589.71 difference within the regular CDBG figures. City narrative · OMB reporting guidance

The City says $102,106.09 in public-service costs was assigned to PY2024 instead of PY2023, and that its HUD field representative approved the correction. We reviewed that City statement, not a separate HUD approval record.

The adjustment appears on line 30 of the PR-26, in the public-service-limit calculation. Line 14, the adjustment to total expenditures, is zero. Subtracting the public-service adjustment from total spending would treat a cap adjustment as an adjustment to total expenditures. This correction does not, by itself, explain the narrative difference. Correction explanation and PR-26, PDF pp. 148–149

Tucson’s CDBG Funding: What Adds Up, and What Still Needs Explaining
We withdrew the earlier $944,972.60 comparison because it combined regular CDBG and CDBG-CV, which are reported separately. The $1,284,589.71 difference within regular CDBG remains unexplained; it does not establish missing funds.
Summary revised:
November 6, 2026, 9:52 a.m. MST (Tucson)
. Original correction history and source dates follow unchanged.
Posted:
November 6, 2026, 7:42 a.m. MST (Tucson)
. Source dates are identified below.
What Did We Find, and Why Does It Matter?
The resource figures and ending balance in Tucson’s CDBG reports add up. The remaining question is more focused: how does the City’s spending narrative connect to the corrected financial report for its regular CDBG program? Federal guidance now helps separate that question from coronavirus-response funding.
Financial summary
·
Spending narrative
·
OMB reporting guidance, PDF p. 61
For residents, the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) can mean home repairs, better public facilities and services for low-income people. Connecting the dollars to completed work helps show what that funding delivered.
City’s description of CDBG-supported work
What Adds Up?
Program income, money generated by CDBG-funded activities, accounts for the previously questioned resource difference. The full financial report also includes money carried over from the previous year:
$5,068,664 annual grant + $349,468 program income = $5,418,132. The income is already included; adding it again would double-count it.
$3,778,221.56 opening balance + $5,418,132 grant and income = $9,196,353.56 in total resources.
$9,196,353.56 resources − $4,717,936.37 expenditures = $4,478,417.19 ending balance.
Those calculations reproduce the City’s resource total and ending balance. The reported balance does not establish money available for new work today.
Corrected PR-26, PDF p. 149
Which Spending Figures Should We Compare?
The Office of Management and Budget’s 2025 Compliance Supplement says the standard PR26 CDBG Financial Summary Report has been restricted to annual formula grants since September 14, 2020. A separate PR26 report covers CDBG-CV, the CARES Act coronavirus-response grants.
OMB reporting guidance, PDF p. 61
That makes the regular CDBG figures the appropriate starting point:
Corrected standard PR-26 expenditures: $4,717,936.37.
CDBG spending stated in the narrative: $3,433,346.66.
Difference requiring reconciliation: $1,284,589.71.
The summary table’s $4,717,936 agrees with the corrected PR-26 after rounding. The narrative says the final CDBG draw occurred after June 30, 2025, which may help explain the difference. But the records reviewed do not show which transactions connect the two figures or establish that timing explains the full amount.
Summary table and narrative, PDF p. 13
·
Corrected PR-26, PDF p. 149
Why Set Aside the Earlier $944,972.60 Comparison?
That calculation subtracted both the $3,433,346.66 CDBG narrative and the $339,616.74 CDBG-CV narrative from the rounded $4,717,936 summary total. It mixed the separately reported grant programs. In light of the federal reporting guidance, it should not be presented as a second comparable spending gap. The question to pursue is the $1,284,589.71 difference within the regular CDBG figures.
City narrative
·
OMB reporting guidance
Does the City’s Separate Correction Resolve This?
The City says $102,106.09 in public-service costs was assigned to PY2024 instead of PY2023, and that its HUD field representative approved the correction. We reviewed that City statement, not a separate HUD approval record.
The adjustment appears on line 30 of the PR-26, in the public-service-limit calculation. Line 14, the adjustment to total expenditures, is zero. Subtracting the public-service adjustment from total spending would treat a cap adjustment as an adjustment to total expenditures. This correction does not, by itself, explain the narrative difference.
Correction explanation and PR-26, PDF pp. 148–149
What Would Make the Picture Clearer?
The corrected PR-26 is available and includes activity and voucher detail. The next step is to connect those records to:
A line-by-line explanation bridging the $3,433,346.66 CDBG narrative to the $4,717,936.37 corrected total, identifying transactions recorded after year-end and keeping CDBG-CV separate.
Commitments, restrictions and later transactions affecting the reported balance.
Completed work and aggregate beneficiary counts from the same reporting period.
PR-26 activity detail, PDF p. 150
How Far Do These Findings Go?
The $1,284,589.71 is an arithmetic difference between reported amounts that still needs a transaction-level explanation. This review does not establish missing funds, currently available assistance or a cost per housing outcome.
This is independent public-record research, not a governmental or certified financial audit. Reporting period: July 1, 2024–June 30, 2025. Corrected PR-26 dated March 13, 2026. City CAPER and OMB guidance rechecked November 6, 2026, Tucson time.

notes: Housing Outcomes and Funding Decisions Historical entry: November 5, 2026 . Newly reviewed records dated July 13 and September 28, 2026. TPCH reports permanent-housing exits for 21 of 36 eligible Housing First PSH leavers (58.33%) and 99 of 177 MDOT street-outreach leavers (55.93%) during July 1, 2025–June 1, 2026. These measures exclude certain destinations, not all participants are counted, and different program types limit comparisons. Both programs are exempt from the grant-expenditure metric; these results do not establish underspending. For an earlier Housing First exit cohort, 7 of 43 people returned to homelessness within 12 months after exiting to permanent housing during June 1, 2024–June 1, 2025. This is a different exit cohort from the 36 leavers above. Underlying data · Methodology, pages 24–27 Separately, the September 28 CoC application reports 50% of one unnamed project’s funding was reallocated for significant underspending. Another kept its funding after documenting expenditures obscured by an eLOCCS access problem. The passage identifies neither project nor links either decision to Housing First or MDOT. Names, dollar amounts and final funding outcomes remain unverified. Application, page 44 Follow-up added November 7, 2026, 9:30 a.m. MST (Tucson) : November 7 records clarify the housing count, grant reduction, financing, El Portal placements and CDBG adoption. The earlier review above is retained as history.

Q-012

How Much Federal Funding Is Documented?
Documented:
HUD’s FY2026 allocation file and Tucson’s FY2027/PY2026 Annual Action Plan agree on four allocations:
Community Development Block Grant (CDBG): $4,962,047 for eligible community-development work, including housing.
HOME: $3,061,840.81 for the Tucson/Pima County consortium.
ESG: $448,998 for Tucson’s Emergency Solutions Grant.
HOPWA: $1,140,597 for housing assistance and services for low-income people with HIV/AIDS and their families.
Together, the allocations total $9,613,482.81. The City separately forecasts $200,000 in CDBG income and $500,000 in HOME income. Each program has its own eligible uses and service area.

The candidate’s earlier date-basis pass reviewed 88 source/evidence entries using 72 newly retrieved public resources and retained originals. A separate consistency pass reviewed 69 funding, question and update entries using existing copies and the public record text. Some findings remain based on HAP statements where an original is unavailable; each result states its check basis. Earlier date checks are retained and not counted as new downloads here.

A wrong HUD download link was found for Tucson SRC-100. The verified Craycroft archive is now linked in this search and supports recorded 2026 certification entries. The old link remains flagged. This does not establish closing, all HUD/RAD approvals or executed assistance contracts.

Unresolved issues include conflicting HOME dataset vintage descriptions, a 2025 column label inside the FY2026 Capital Fund formula workbook, undated questions/indexes, source-review-only Updates, and unavailable originals. These issues are shown explicitly rather than filled with inferred dates. Date checks do not resolve the stated evidence gaps.

Across both regions, 187 of 215 entries have a labeled source, event, publication or coverage year. 28 have no established primary year. Funding uses a separate field. 16 funding entries have a stated period and 14 have an unverified active period. Source, event and check dates do not fill that funding filter.

Funding periods remain qualified: planned competitions, draft reporting, composite scopes and unsigned agreement terms do not establish continuous operation or completed spending. Known source/event dates and cited unverified leads are shown separately and do not silently fill the fiscal/program-year filter.

Separate official Maricopa materials now corroborate HOME competition PY2027–28 and the December 8, 2026 deadline before 5 p.m. The original packet bodies and exact financial estimates remain unverified.
